newsitem.title: Belgium: EU ministers defend unemployment policies.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers defend unemployment policies.

text.p: European Union finance ministers, under fire over mounting unemployment in Europe, stressed on Monday that the path to greater jobs growth rested with structural reform of their labour markets.
Meeting against the backdrop of record unemployment in Germany, the ministers said they expected the EU's struggling economy to show signs of renewed vigour, a development aided by a stronger dollar.
"The increase in the value of the dollar is very important to us," Dutch finance minister Gerrit Zalm told a news conference.

Zalm said an expected rebound in EU growth to 2.3 percent this year from 1.6 percent in 1996 was still on the cards, but he acknowledged the high rate of unemployment was a challenge that required further structural reforms.
"In general, the situation is unsatisfactory concerning unemployment," Zalm said. "The only correct response...are structural reforms."
The focus of the ministerial meeting was the European Commission's annual economic report, which urges governments to adopt greater labour market flexibility to fight rising unemployment.
The EU executive forecast last week that faster economic growth would have only a limited impact on the current 10.8 percent EU jobless rate.
"The moderate strengthening of employment growth in the Community in the coming years is expected to be sufficient to achieve only a modest reduction in unemployment," the report said.
Europe's jobless problem has been highlighted as Germany, the EU's main economic engine, struggles with nearly 4.7 million unemployed, the highest level since the 1930s.
The record unemployment rate has raised doubts over Bonn's ability to cut expenditure and bring its budget deficit within the Maastricht Treaty's target.
Under growing political pressure, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel has yet to announce how he plans to deal with an expected shortfall in revenue.
Independent economists have estimated the high unemployment rate would add between 10 billion marks and 18 billion marks ($6 to $11 billion) to German government spending.
But on Monday, German State Secretary for Finance Juergen Stark said Bonn was prepared to do whatever was necessary to meet its 2.9 percent deficit-to-GDP target in 1997.

"The 2.9 percent is a carefully calculated figure in which we have already considered all recognisable risks," he told a news conference. "If we have further decreases in tax revenues we will take further corrective measures."

Fending off concerns that Germany might not be able to meet the preconditions of a common currency, Zalm said a stronger dollar and low long-term interest rates should help offset the negative impact of higher unemployment.

The link between the drive by EU governments towards a common currency and unemployment has become more controversial, with many believing that politicians are being handicapped in their ability to follow pro-labour market policies.
Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean Claude Juncker played down any connection between fiscal austerity and joblessness, however, stressing the need for new policies.
"We have to bring down non-wage labour costs and labour taxes," Juncker, who is also finance minister, told reporters.

Separately, EU finance ministers endorsed the efforts that Belgium has made towards meeting the Maastricht Treaty's criteria on deficits, interest rates and inflation -- the main requirements for joining a single currency.
In March, the ministers will review new economic convergence plans from Germany and France. ($ = 1.69 German Marks)
